title: The Morality of the Ramayana: a Rejoinder
html:
The Morality of the Ramayana—A Rejoinder.

BY

MR. T. PONNAMBALAM PILLAI, M. R. A. S.

In preparing my paper on the Morality of Ramayana, to the “Malabar Quarterly Review” I intended to interpret the views of the late professor Sundaram Pillai, to a larger circle of readers than the Tamil article, in the Tamilian Antiquary, (No. 2), was able to command, in order to elicit rational criticism, in the interests of the Southern Indian History. As education advances it is but natural that investigations into the history of one’s own land, particularly if it is enveloped in mystery, should be made. At all events, such a spirit pervades at present the minds of all educated men both in Southern India and Ceylon, where most of the scenes in the Ramayana have been laid. If in the course of such a legitimate enquiry old ideas are exploded, all right thinking people ought to welcome such a healthy change, and sympathise with the workers in their difficult labours. In the place of such generous treatment, I least expected a furious, but a pointless attack, from the pen of Mr. Sadasiva Iyer, the talented Chief Justice of Travancore, who is known for his perfect equanimity of temper, and who until now never permitted it to be ruffled by anything, as became an arbiter of Justice in the Highest Court of the kingdom. I also regret, that in the heat of the fight he should have so forgotten himself, as to introduce into the arena of discussion, a large number of unparliamentary expressions (about 40 in number besides unlimited inuendoes), thus following the vernacular controversies he has condemned after taking exception to my using certain strong terms; and as a crowning act, that he should have suggested, that some evil spirit, probably from the nether world, impelled me to set my pen to the article in question.

What I regret more than anything, is his reference to my motives, and the introduction of politics into the review of my paper. In the first place, it is hard that I should be denounced, as attacking a class, if in the course of making a statement of certain historical facts, it is placed in an unfavourable light. In the next place, it was in no light-heartedmood, or with the object of ridiculing the worship of Rama, that I penned the article which Mr. Sadasiva Iyer criticises. I should perhaps have added the warning with which Mr. V.P. Subramania Mudaliar, the author of the Tamil version prefaced it, viz. that it was only an historical aspect of the question.

It is however gratifying to me that my reviewer credits me with the Saiva Siddhantha faith. The broad and cosmopolitan principles which it inculcates are embodied in the following stanza of the Kunda-Purana (கக்ஷ காண்டய, கந்தவிரதப்படலம்.)

எவ்வெவார் தம்மையேனும் யாவரே பெனினும் போற்றின்,
அவ்வவரிடமாக் விசாண்டே, யவர்க்கருள் தருவாய் போற்றி,
மெய்வரு தெளிவிலுண்ணை வெளிப்படவுணர்ந்துள் ளோர்க்குத்,
தெய்வத போக முத்தி சிறப்பொடு தருவாய் போற்றி.”

“ Whosoever may worship Thee in whatsoever aspect, Thou wilt present Thyself as such, and grant him grace. To those that understand Thee aright, Thou wouldst grant beatitude gracefully. I adore such a Deity.” If I adhere to these views (and I assure my readers that I do) I cannot consistently trifle with the faith inculcated in the Ramayana, and will not directly, or indirectly, consciously or unconsciously, indulge in such a treatment as that with which I have been fathered by Mr. Sadasiva Iyer; though it is a difficult thing to question the absurdities and supernaturalisms that have been smuggled into it by some of its deluded votaries.

To construct a reliable history of Southern India constant reference has to be made to the Ramayana, one of the few sources of ancient record. But dealing, as it does, with hoary antiquity, garbed as the facts are in our inherent national hyperbole, drawn as the imageries are in such a way as to border upon mythology, and unrestrained as the chroniclers are in their indulgence to the fullest extent, in the license which poetry permits, it should be the endeavour of every sane man to allow the facts to be treated as historical truths, to be put to a crucial scientific test. It is my humble, but my firm belief, that this test consists in courting healthy and open criticism of all doubtful facts. This is an experience. not at all foreign to my critic, who had large experience as a Judicial Officer. In performing this task, if I am charged with the offence of disturbing the established faith, my reply is that the end justifies the means.

Now as to politics. I repeat that I regret the introduction of this subject into the discussion. I have always had a natural disinclination to discuss it, and the unfortunate condition of India at the present moment makes any reference to the topic unsavory. If I am compelled to enter the lists, Mr. Sadasiva Aiyar alone is responsible for my doing so. In the course of his criticism, he says that the delay in the introduction of Lord Morley's reforms is due to the conduct of people like my humble self. But as is evident from the published reports, it is due to that generous spirit which prompted the benign British Government to launch the whole scheme. Here I must digress for a moment to explain myself and to enable Mr. Sadasiva Aiyar to refresh his memory in the study of ancient history.* .....

I think I should make one more preliminary observation, before proceeding to the discussion of the main subject, in order to correct what I may term, a historical solecism. Mr. Sadasiva Iyer speaks in a patronising tone saying that certain Dravidian friends of his, ought to be counted as Brahmins and Kshatrias and I believe if he had the power he would have raised them to that dignity. He further adds that there is a large infusion of Aryan blood amongst the Dravidians, but failed to state the reverse. It has already been pointed out,* that when the Aryans entered Northern India, they did so as conquerors and not as peaceful emigrants, though at a later stage they became identified with the races already in possession of the land. But it was the other way when they entered Southern India, and they were enabled to do so only by the sufferance of the Dravidians. I make this statement on the authority of the Ramayana itself. During his exile, when Rama travelled from place to place he took care to ascertain, where to get lodgings for himself and his two relations from friendly people, and how to protect themselves from man and beast (vide canto 54 Ayodyakanda). Again the fact that Agastia, the sage, was constantly subject to attacks from such individuals, as Sutha, the husband of Tadaka, Tadaka herself, and her son Mareecha (canto 25, Balakanda), that the sages at Chitrakuta had to abandon their dwellings owing to the ill-treatment of Kara of Janasthana, that Rama was able only to hear their complaints and sympathise with them (canto 116, Ayodyakanda) and that he had clandestinely to make an alliance with Sugriva at the Rishyamuka Ranges, while Vali more powerful than Ravana was holding undisputed sway over Kishkintha (canto 10, Kishkinthakanda), go to show that that the Aryans were dependent upon the pleasure of, and seekers of favour from, the permanent dwellers of the soil. In these circumstances, they would only have been too glad to enter into close relationship with the all-powerful natives. Mr. Sadasiva Iyer makes a serious admission. For he says “that many conquered and indigenous races belonging to an earlier civilization must of course have been taken into Aryan caste system. Some of the more enlightened and religious members belonging to such indigenous races, were incorporated as even Kshatrias and Vysias”; and I ask why not as Brahmins?

The statement made by Mr. Sadasiva Iyer is an historical truth, as the result of the evolution of the society, when an emigrant people mix with a resident population. It has been authoritatively established, that the Dravidians were not the indigenous races of Southern India. They belong to an earlier wave of emigration, and in all probability, the first batch of them crossed over by sea from Western Asia, as is evident from their skill as sailors. Notwithstanding the nick-names of giants and monkeys given to them by the Aryans, the description given in the Ramayana of their cities and buildings, the high standard of morality observed by the generality of them, and the state of efficiency and discipline in which their armies were maintained, go to show the high level of civilization attained by them. This was their condition when the Aryans crossed the Indus (vide Vedic India Page 291). After centuries when they advanced towards the south, though there were the usuai bickerings in the beginning, both the races became reconciled to each other, and identified with one another, so as to form a single nation. From what has fallen from Kiplar, a poet of the last Academy at Madura, it seems that the caste system was introduced into Southern India at a late stage. From the above it is evident that both the races were fused together into one, and subsequently the division of caste was initiated. In that case the Dravidians must have become not only Kshatrias and Vysias, but also Brahmins, as was the case with the Non-aryan Indians of Northern India like Viswamithra, Vyasa and Valmeeki. There are modern parallels to this historic fact in other parts of the world, and mention may be made of the case of Boers and British settlers in South Africa. From these facts, it is patent that not only Aryan blood flows freely in the veins of the Dravidians, but the reverse is also the case. I cannot but observe here, that I was compelled to discuss this question at this length by Mr. Sadasiva Iyer, and in doing so, I have not intended offence to anybody.

Before entering upon the main question, I must at the outset point out that when I penned my article on the Ramayana, I had expressly stated that I had given an English garb to the ideas of Professor Sundaram Pillai as clothed in Tamil by my friend Mr. V. P. Subramania Mudaliar. As the late professor and myself have since been taken to task, I propose to accept all responsibility and with the assistance of Mr. Subramania Mudaliar, to meet, as much as it lies in our power, the attack conceived and levelled in an unfair and illiberal spirit by my critic, though not with that clearness of thought, and felicity of diction, which characterised the writings of the late Mr. Sundaram Pillai.

It has been admitted on all hands that the late lamented professor was a profound scholar, an archæologist, and a thinker of no mean order. If, therefore, on a set of given facts he arrived at a conclusion, which satisfies any reasonable mind, it is hard to find fault with him. With regard to his want of faith in the Ramayana, it continued up to the day of his death, as will be seen from the introduction to the Tamilian Antiquary, No. 2, by Mr. J. M. Nallaswamy Pillai, B. A., B. L. I may also state here that in this disbelief he stood in good company, for Mr. R. C. Dutt, whose recent irreparable loss is mourned throughout the length and breadth of India, whose right to fame as a scholar and savant of European reputation, is greater than that of Mr. Sadasiva Iyer, and whose admiration for the sublime portions of the Ramayana is second to none, has delivered himself as follows.

“Like the Mahabaratha, the Ramayana is utterly value-less as a narrative of historical events and incidents. As in the Mahabaratha, so in the Ramayana, the heroes are myths pure and simple.”

“Sita, the field furrow, had received divine honours from the time of the Rig Veda, and had been worshipped as a goddess. When cultivation gradually spread in Southern India, it was not difficult to invent a political myth that Sita was carried to the South. And when she is goddess and women,—the noblest creation of human imagination,—had acquired a distinct and lovely individuality, she was naturally described as the daughter of the holiest and most learned king on record, Janaka of the Videhas.”

“ But who is Rama, described in the epic as Sita’s husband and the king of the Kosalas? The later Puranas tell us that he was an incarnation of Vishnu, but Vishnu himself had not risen to prominence at the time of which we are speaking. Indra was still the chief of the Gods of the Epic period. And in the Sutra literature (e. g. Paraskara Grihya Sutra II, 17, 9) we learn that Sita, the furrow goddess, is the wife of Indra. Is it then an untenable conjecture that Rama, the hero of the Ramayana, is in his original conception, like Arjuna the hero of the Mahabaratha, only a new edition of Indra battling with the demons of drought. The myth of Indra has thus been mixed up with the epic which describes as an historic war in Northern India, and with the epic which describes the historic conquest of Southern India.” (Dutt’s Early Hindu Civilization, Vol. I, page 138.)

As the morality of the Ramayana rests chiefly on the conduct of the leading Aryan heroes and their confederates, I have touched on the following points in my first article, though incidentally minor questions have been discussed.

(1) The conduct of Vâli, or Bâli and Sugríva, towards each other, and their character.

(2) The nature of the alliance between the latter and Rama.

(3) The conduct of Ravana and Vibhishana, towards each other, and their character.

(4) The nature of the alliance between the latter and Rama.

(5) The existence of the beings called Rakshasas, Asuras, Devas and Vânaras.

Mr. Sadasiva Iyer, who has discovered in my paper an attack levelled against his class, and has therefore taken up the gauntlet on their behalf, begins by stating that he does not propose to refute my arguments in detail. The reason assigned for this omission is the want of time—a subterfuge generally adopted by less subtle things. To my mind it is impossible to meet some of the questions raised by my friends, and the presumption of the omission is no doubt in my favour. He not only passes over most of the points noted above, but altogether refrains from dwelling on the existence or otherwise of the beings called Rakshasas (Giants), Asurars (Demons), Devas (Celestials) and Vanarars (Men with tails), and raises certain side issues such as the relationship between Ravana and Tataka and the overlordship of Janasthana and Dandakaranya.

One of the greatest charges levelled against us is, that we have misrepresented matters, by referring to information that does not find a place in the Ramayana of Valmeeki. Mr. Sadasiva Iyer refers to Thulasiram's, Kamban's, and Elu-thachan's, and other renderings of the epic. Referring to the same subject, my friend Mr. Subramania Mudaliar says, that though the Ramayana has been translated into all the Indian languages, whenever a person speaks of it, it is generally supposed to be that of the Valmeeki (vide p. iii, preface No. 2 Tamilian Antiquary). It is in that strain we have spoken of it, and as far as I have investigated, there is no material difference between the original work and the Ramayana of Kamban with which my friends and myself are familiar. Even granting that there were misquotations, with regard to the particular items referred to by Mr. Sadasiva Iyer, I do not think that they have affected in any way the main questions. Notwithstanding the taunts and inuendoes directed at us by Mr. Sadasiva Iyer, all right-minded people will agree in thinking that the story of the Aryan Chronicler should be accepted with caution. For, in my first article I pointed out that it was a partisan account and the object of the thesis was to enhance the reputation of his compeers at the expense of their adversaries.

With this introduction I shall deal with the various questions at issue. But it will be more convenient to dispose of some of the minor points—particularly the overlordship of Dandakaranya and Janasthana, and the relationship between Ravana and Tataka,—before dwelling with the main ones, as Mr. Sadasiva Iyer seems to attach much importance to their determination.

With regard to the first, Mr. Sadasiva Iyer firmly believes that both provinces were under the suzerainty of the empire of Dasaratha, and in support of the contention quotes Canto V. of the Balakanda. In doing so he says, “that the entire land of India belonged to the Solar Race of kings”, and he adds “ that the Ikshvaku’s race owned the whole of the land surrounded by seas.” There can be no doubt that Mr. Sadasiva Iyer intended to convey identically the same meaning by the two extracts under marks of quotation, but the words employed do not import it. The first means that the Solar dynasty reigned over the whole of India, while the other means over the whole world. On looking through the metric translation of Valmeeki into English by professor Griffiths, and that of Mr. Natesa Sastry into Tamil prose, I find that the poet meant the whole world. If his words are to be construed literally, the undoubted existence of a Chaldean, an Assyrian, a Babylonian, a Persian, an Egyptian, and a Chinese Empire in times of yore must be untrue, and the mythological imageries of a rhapsodist alone should be held as true. But I have my doubts as to whether the spirit of the age would permit the whole-sale swallowing of patent absurdities of this kind.

There is enough of internal evidence in the Ramayana itself to prove that the Kosala empire did not extend to Southern India, so as to include Dandakaranya and Janasthana. The following are some of the facts which may be urged in support of the contention :—

(1) That from the same authority quoted by Mr. Sadasiva Iyer (vide canto V of Balakanda) Kosala was a small kingdom, on the banks of Sarayu.

(2) That Janaka, king of Mithila, was of the same status as that of Dasaratha and was not a tributary sovereign (as my critic would have us believe) to the Emperor of India. (vide canto 70 and 71 of Balakanda).

(3) That the abject manner in which Dasaratha in conjunction with the sages, entreated Parasurama not to molest his son Rama, on his way back to Ayodhyah, after his marriage with Sita, does not show that he was the all-powerful Emperor of India (vide canto 65, Balakanda.)

(4) That when Rama, the heir to the throne, passed the confines of Kosala after his exile, he had to receive instructions with regard to the geographical position of the places he had to visit and the people inhabiting them. This ignorance is inexcusable in the future Emperor (vide cantos 54 and 55, Ayodhyah Kanda, and the earlier cantos of Aranyakanda.)

(5) The helpless condition in which Rama—the avenger of the wrongs of everybody under the sun—found himself when the sages resident at Chitrakuta complained to him of illtreatment offered to them by Kara—a cousin of Ravana and chief minister of Surpanaka—sallying forth his post at Janasthana, and the complacent manner in which he was compelled to witness their departure to a safe retreat at a great distance (vide canto 116, Ayodhyah Kanda).

(6) That there was a settled Government at Janasthana coupled with Dandakaranya, at the head of which was Surpanaka with Kara as her chief adviser, and Dushana as Commander-in-chief of an armed force of 14,000 picked men. (Vide cantos 12 to 30 Aranyakanda, and canto 29 Uttarakanda.)

(7) That when Akamban and Surpanaka sped to Lanka from Janasthana and reported to Ravana that

“Rama was there to strike and slay
“By him, O! King of high estate,
“Is Janasthana left desolate.”

Canto 31, Aranyakanda.

“Know Rama with his conquering arm
“Has freed the saints, from dread of harm,
“Has smitten Janasthana and made
“Asylum safe in Dandaka’s shade.”

Canto 33, Aranyakanda.

their feeling was that the provinces were subject to the rule of Ravana.

(8) That on being informed of the desolate condition in which Janasthana “that feared no hate of foes” and Dandakaranya were laid, his feeling enquiries, quoted below, serve as an index of his sway.

“What fool has dared, already dead
“Strike Janasthana, the general dread?

Canto 31, Aranyakanda.

Who is this Rama.....what purpose led to Dandaka forest, hard to tread?

Canto 34, Aranyakanda.

.....did Rama seek the shade of Janasthana with Indra’s aid?

Canto 31, Aranyakanda.

(9) That in discussing the subject with Mareecha, the great anxiety with which he declaims thus :—

“My generous, the bravest of my band
“Are slain by Rama’s vigorous hand
“And Janasthana that feared no hate
“Of foes, is rendered desolate.”

Canto 31, Aranyakanda.

exhibits the sense of his authority.

The foregoing facts prove clearly:—

(1) That the kingdom of Kosala was limited in extent.

(2) That there were kings of the same status as Dasaratha and they were not tributaries to him, and he could not therefore have been Emperor of India.

(3) That Janasthana and Dandakaranya were under the undisputed sway of Ravana, and the least interference from outside exasperated him.

Now let us see whether there is any evidence, outside the Ramayana. It has already been noted that Janaka, the father of Sita, was the contemporary of Dasaratha. According to historical researches Videhas, Kosalas and Kasis were powerful and civilised kingdoms established east of the Ganges, and Janaka, the ruler of the first named of them was the most powerful of all the kings. "That monarch had not only established his power in the farthest confines of the Hindu dominions in India," but had also started "speculations enquiring" about the "destination of the soul, and the nature of the supreme being," so as to find a permanent place for himself in the Upanishads (vide Dutt's Early Hindu civilization Vol., I, Book II, Chapter III.) If Dasaratha was a contemporary of Janaka, the latter was certainly a more powerful king, and if an emperor was to be elected the choice would certainly have fallen on him. With regard to the identity of Janaka there is no doubt, for the pedigree given in Canto 71 of the Balakanda makes no mention of any other king of the line by the same name. But the most important fact that has to be determined is the extent of the Hindu Aryan world at the time we are speaking of. From chapter V of the same volume and book, it is seen that proceeding from the banks of the Indus on the west, the Aryans had settled themselves down in the tracts watered by the Ganges and the Jumna by the year 1000 B.C. and the kingdom referred to above was the newest and the latest of the Hindu kingdoms. "Beyond this wide tract of Hindu kingdoms lay the whole extent of India yet unexplored or rather unconquered by the Aryans, and peopled by various aboriginal tribes. A wide belt of this non-aryan tract surrounding the Hindu world to the east, south and west was becoming known to the Hindus about the close of the epic period. South Behar, Malwa and a portion of the Deccan, the regions to the south of the Rajaputana desert, formed a wide semicircular belt of country as yet not hinduised, but becoming gradually known to the Hindus" (Chapter IV of the same Book). Thus the limits of the Aryan world did not go beyond the Vindhya Range.

This state of things existed, as I have already pointed out, about 1000 B. C. We must now see when further expansion of the Aryan India was made. Boudhayana who flourished much later, probably about the sixth century B. C., and who was one of the founders of the Sutra-school fixes the following boundaries as those of Aryavarta or the country of the Aryans, viz.

North.....Hymalayas.
East.....Behar.
South.....Vindhya Ranges.
West.....The Saraswati.

and prescribes a penalty in the form of a sacrifice for the absolution of the sin of crossing them (Boudhayana I., 1 and 2, as quoted by Dutt Vol. 1. page 214). Thus for religious more than political reasons, which were subordinated, the limits of Aryan India were not permitted to be extended beyond the Vindhya Mountains.

At the time of the invasion of India about the year 327 B.C. by Alexander the Great, Chandraguptha was the most powerful Aryan king, and his dominions included most of the portions of Northern India which are at present ruled over by four Lieutenant Governors and a Chief Commissioner. Portions of Bengal, Orissa and the Central Provinces formed the Kalingah kingdom, and south of it was the Andhrah kingdom extending up to the banks of the Krishna. Later on, when the great Asoka succeeded his father, the son of Chandraguptha, he absorbed all the surrounding territories; but the limits of his empire did not advance further than those of Andhrah, for his Edicts No, II places the Chola, the, Pandya and Chera kingdoms beyond the frontier of the Empire, and they are treated as foreign and independent potentates.

Thus, step by step, I have striven to show that the Kosala Empire did not reach that limit claimed by Mr. Sadasiva Iyer, at any time; if, at such a late period as the middle of the third century B. C., the limit of the territories of a powerful monarch could not have gone beyond the river Krishna, it stands to reason that at an earlier period when there was no desire for conquest, and the chivalrous feats attributed to Rama were mostly in self-defence, Dandakaranya and Janasthana did not form part of the imaginary empire of Dasaratha. I cannot but remark here, with greater men than myself, that Valmiki was not a contemporary of Rama, and in elaborating a story he had heard from Narada and supplemented by Brahma, he drew as much as possible from his imagination, and was therefore guilty of the sin of anachronism.

With regard to Tadaka, there is no doubt, that she was originally a Gandharva woman—a name given by the Aryans to some of the non-aryan races; but, as pointed out by Mr. Sadasiva Iyer, she laterly embraced the faith of the Rakshasas with her whole family, and became identified with them. According to Valmeeki she was the wife of a Yaksha by name Sutha, and as he wantonly destroyed the garden of Agastya, he was reduced to ashes by him. Enraged at this she and her son Mareecha repaired to the scene of this catastrophe to wreak vengeance, but on their appearance they were cursed to assume the form of Rakshasas. After this event she went on with her depredations, as usual with women of her class and strength; and proved a terror to the sages resorting to the forests of Malasam and Karusam, not far away from the Southern banks of the Ganges. Amongst others she molested Visvamithra in the performance of his great sacrifice. The first mission of the youthful Rama was to destroy this giantess (vide cantos 24 and 25, Balakanda.)

After this event, we next hear of Mareecha in Janasthana in the service of Ravana. As belonging to the class of Rakshasas, Tadaka and Mareecha had community of interest with Ravana and other fellow Rakshasas. As Tadaka was a princess and a leading member of one of the clans of Rakshasas, it is but natural that her death, by the hand of Rama, must have been working in the mind of Ravana, and if he had taken any steps to avenge it, it would have been justifiable. The Tamil poet Kamban who drew his inspiration from three Sanskrit works, including that of Valmiki, states that after the death of his father, Mareecha and his brother were adopted by Sumali, the maternal grandfather of Ravana, as his children, and thus they became the uncles of Ravana (Vide Balakandam). In this case Tadaka was in the relationship of a grand parent to Ravana. But this is a matter that does not affect the main subject of controversy.

Bâli, or Vali, Sugriva, and Rama.—In discussing their character, it appears to me necessary to state the facts at length as recorded by Valmiki, that there may be no misconception. Of the two brothers, Vali was the elder and Sugriva the younger. The former was sitting on the throne of his ancestors, at the time of the visit of Rama and Lakshmana, by right of primogeniture, and Sugriva was in exile in the Rishyamukha Hills. Long before his banishment, when he was living with his brother on friendly terms, on a certain night, an Asura by name Mâyâvi repaired to the gates of Kishkinda and challenged Vali to fight, owing to some love affair. In spite of the advice of all interested in him, including Sugriva, he accepted the challenge, and ran out to meet him. Out of affection and regard, Sugriva followed him. At the sight of the brothers, the demon fled for his life, and took refuge in a cave. Disappointed as Vali was, he was not prepared to give up the chase. He turned to his brother and asked him to watch the mouth of the cave carefully, till his return. Sugriva tried to dissuade him from his impetuous course, but Vali was inexorable and made his brother swear by his feet that he would carry out his injunctions. He tarried at the entrance to the cave, for one full year, and the only signs of life there were the roaring sound of Mayavi, and the streaming of frothy blood from the cave. Sugriva concluded that his brother was dead, shut up the cave with a stone “as huge as a hill”, performed his last rites, returned to Kishkinda and refrained from mentioning the facts to anybody. But the ministers of Vali learned them, and, in consultation with the people, installed him on the throne of his brother. While he was thus reigning, Vali returned to the mouth of the cave, found it barred, and called Sugriva by name. But as there was no response he was in a state of despair. With a great effort he kicked away the stone and betook himself to Kishkinda. On the reappearance of his brother, Sugriva surrendered the crown, explained to him that it was set on his head, for the defence of the kingdom, tried to propitiate him, and besought him to forgive him. But Vali was not appealed. He slew the ministers who were instrumental in placing his brother on the throne, deprived Sugriva of his wife and banished him from the kingdom with only a strip of cloth round his loins. From that time, up to the moment of the arrival of Rama and Lakshmana, he was living on the Rishiyamuka Hills, which Vali was debarred from approaching, owing to an imprecation on the part of sage Mathanga (Cantos 9 and 10, Kishkindha kanda).

After the abduction of Sita, when the brothers were at their wits' end to find out its author, and her whereabouts, they appealed to Kabandha who had assumed the celestial form of Danu, and he directed them to go to Kishkindha, and seek the aid of Sugriva, who was in the same plight as Rama was (vide canto 73 Aranya Kanda). On their arrival at the Malaya hills in the Mathanga forests, the brothers were anxious to seek an interview with Sugriva, but he espying them from a distance took them for Vali's spies in disguise, and took the necessary precautions to guard himself and his friends against any untoward danger. After, however, holding counsel with his brethren in adversity (for there were some who were sent into exile at the same time with Sugriva, such as Hanuman, Nalan, Neelan, &c.,) he made up his mind to depute Hanuman to go to the youthful heroes, learn the object of their mission, and secure if possible their assistance in encompassing the death of Vali and ending his tyrannical rule. His mission was successful. Hanuman went in the guise of mendicant, reconnoitered the position, and finding that there was nothing suspicious, he informed them of the object of his visit, which was of course quite welcome to them. Rama and Lakshmana at once, in the company of Hanuman, proceeded to the residence of Sugriva, and concluded a defensive and offensive alliance. The object of this was, that Rama should bring about the death of Vali, and place Sugriva on his throne. The latter was on his part to assist him in the recovery of Sita (Cantos 2 to 6, Kishkindhakanda).

The next step was the fulfilment of the promises. Impelled by Rama, Sugriva led his friends to Kishkindha. and while they remained concealed in a dense wood, he raised the usual war cry and challenged Vali to combat. He accepted the challenge, fought with his usual bravery, and discomfitted Sugriva, who having had no aid from Rama, fled into the Mathanga forests. As has already been pointed out, Vali was compelled to give up pursuit, owing to the interdict placed against him to enter it. Rama, Lakshmana and other friends followed Sugriva to the grove. On their approach, he taunted Rama with practising deceit on him, by failing to perform his part of the promise. Rama explained, that while the brothers were fighting the dual, he was not able to detect a shade of difference between them, and he had therefore to refrain from discharging his arrow at Vali for fear of killing him. In order to distinguish one from the other, he directed Lakshmana to throw round the neck of Sugriva a wreath of creepers with crimson flowers on, and desired him to go back to Kishkindha and challenge Vali again for combat. While he readily did so, Rama and his brother remained in the sacred grove, watching what was going on in the battle-field (canto 12, Kishkindhakanda.) Vali did not hesitate to encounter Sugriva a second time, notwithstanding the entreaties of his chief and favourite Queen Tara, not to fight his brother on that inauspicious day. He passed out of the portals of his palace, and took up the gauntlet. The combat was fought most fiercely, but with varying success, till at length Rama observing his friend staggering under the blows of “ the conquering foe” laid his hand on his bow strings, and aimed his arrow at the breast of Vali. It pierced his heart unswervingly, and with the arrow implanted in his heart, he reeled and fell. (Canto 16, Kishkindhakanda.)

I have given this account at length as it is not available to the ordinary reader. As Mr. Sadasiva Iyer is anxious to justify the conduct of Rama and Sugriva, he should be in a position to judge for himself. The first and foremost breach of propriety on the part of Sugriva was the desertion of his post. He had the whole kingdom at his back, and he was consequently in a position to command all conveniences for staying at the mouth of the cave, for any length of time. If he was tired of his duty, he could at least have put some of his trusted followers at the post such as Hanuman, Nala, and Neelan, who later on in the war with Ravana performed great exploits. In the next place the indecent haste with which he arrived at the conclusion, that his brother was dead, does not prove his bona fides. He relied upon conjectures rather than satisfying himself with practical proof. His intimate friend and Lieutenant Hanuman, was known to possess prodigious powers, so that he could assume any shape, attain any speed and stalk over the sphere—the celestial and nether worlds included. An individual like this could have been sent at the head of a search party, before Sugriva assumed regal powers. Thirdly, his closing the cavern with a huge stone, does not demonstrate that he was innocent. That act only goes to show, that he did not wish Vali his brother and king to return. Fourthly, his silence was more than criminal. If he had given the necessary information to those more interested than himself, such as the queens of Vali and his son Angada, they would have set people to look for him. Lastly even granting that the interests of the kingdom required the presence of a king, his duty was to place his nephew on the throne, and act as his guardian, or the regent. The will of the people as suggested by Mr. Sadasiva Iyer had nothing to do in a country where the law of Primogeniture prevailed, and this fact was admitted to Rama by Sugriva. It was, moreover, decided by the behest of Rama, to make Angada the heir-apparent to the throne, and Sugriva implicitly obeyed his wishes. The late Mr. Dutt has put the matter most graphically thus.

“Gallant Angada, son of Bali is in regal
duties trained

“Ruling partner of thy Empire to be
valiant prince ordained

“Eldest son of the eldest brother such
the maxim we own

“Worthy of his father’s kingdom doth
ascend his father’s throne.”

(Page III Dutt’s Ramayana.)

It seems to me that Rama himself felt the justice of his claim and desired to make amends for the injustice that had been perpetrated. It will be seen from the facts marshalled above, that any amount of white-washing of Sugriva, because he was a partisan of the Aryans, will not clear him of his sin, and that, when Mr. Dutt said.—“Bali was a great king amongst the non-Aryans, but Sugriva thirsted after his kingdom,” he stated the truth (vide Ancient Hindu Civilization Vol. 1, p. 141.) Thus the cause espoused by Rama was not a righteous one, and he was impelled to act thus by self-interest.

Now we will examine the conduct of Rama, and see how he comes out of the ordeal. When his shaft struck Vali it did not kill him instantly. Before he breathed his last he had the satisfaction of knowing who the author of his death was and what justification he had in bringing it about. After Vali was laid prostrate, Rama and Lakshmana approached him, probably with the object of admiring his valour. Addressing them with all respect, he tauntingly enquired, what fame they had secured by secretly compassing his death, and without openly fighting with him in the field, as a serpent does to death a sleeping man, while he had done them no harm knowingly or unknowingly. (Canto 17, Kishkindhakandam.)

In reply Rama advanced two grounds, viz:—

1. That the country governed by Vali was subject to the authority of king Baratha as a descendent of Ikshvaku, and he (Rama) as his representative was justified in administering condign punishment to him (Vali) for ravishing the wife of his younger brother Sugriva.

2. That as he (Vali) was an animal, a royal personage such as he was, was justified in hunting him down.

(Canto 18, Kishkindhakanda.)

With regard to the first, I have taken some trouble to prove that the Ikshvaku Empire did not extend to southern India, and that such a condition was impossible in the light of the circumstances existing at the time. On this ground, the authority of king Bharatha could not have been extended to Kishkindha, and much less could Rama have acted as his representative. In the next place even granting that Bharatha exercised suzerainty over Kishkindha, where was the authority on which Rama acted?

(1) As an exile he was a state prisoner, and as such he was debarred from taking part in matters of state. The fact that Rama declined to be present at the coronation of Sugriva, on the ground that he was forbidden by his father to enter any city or country, during the foreteen years of his exile, (Canto 26, Kishkindhakandam) confirms the statement.

(2) If Rama had been in a position to receive a mandate of this kind from the Emperor Bharatha, the first thing he would have done would have been to seek his aid in the recovery of Sitá.

(3) It is curious that a person who was unable to help himself should interfere in state matters.

Lastly, of the two main arguments advanced by Rama, one cuts the other asunder. For, if Vali could be hunted down as a beast of the field by a royal sportsman, it would be unfair to enforce the standard of morality maintained in human society amongst quadrupeds.

Vâli—The view taken by my friends and myself, after removing the allegorical veil, is that Vali was a powerful Dravidian king, that when he had to leave his kingdom on an expedition of conquest, he left the reins of Government in the hands of Sugriva, but on his return he found him, surrounded by a number of evil advisers refusing to restore the Government of the country. On this he had to fight his brother, kill some of his followers, and send to exile Sugriva and the rest of them. At the same time he detained the wife of Sugriva as a prize of war and was justified by the code of warfare existing at that time. Here we may cite a modern parallel in the act of the great Napolean after the battle of Austerlitz. After his fall, Valmiki himself has detected in Vali a great and high souled king (Canto 17, Kishkindhakanda). His great piety is referred to in canto 39, of the Uttarakanda. He was above all a very generous man. For when he banished Sugriva it was quite in his power to have put him to death. But his fraternal love and his usual kindly nature prevented him from taking that extreme step. (Canto 24, Kishkindhakanda.) Again we find that when his favourite queen Tara counselled him against fighting his brother and urged him to live in peace with him, he said that he would once more crush Sugriva's pride and thus teach another lesson, but would not destroy him (Canto 16, Kishkindhakanda). To the very last his generous nature would not permit him to think that Rama would be guilty of any iniquity, and that if he did him any harm it would be in fair fight. But such a trait of character appears to be inherent in the family. For, during the war between the Celestials and the Rakshasas, Malyavan had to point out the time-honoured morality of the Kshatrias and taunt Narayana thus: 'Like a base wight thou slayest us desisting from fight and exercised with fear.' (Canto 8, Uttarakanda).

With regard to the observation of Mr. Sadasiva Iyer that Valmiki did not keep back facts unfavourable to the Aryans, I have only to remark that it is always a difficult task to conceal truth. And he has also made much of the counsel of Tara. It will be seen from Canto 15 of the Kishkindhakanda that the following were the points urged by Tara against fighting Sugriva on the second occasion:

  1. (1) That the day was inauspicious;
  2. (2) That Rama was invincible in war and saintly in character;
  3. (3) That it was the duty of the elder brother to protect the younger.

There is therefore nothing about the justness of the cause espoused by Rama, unless the inference is drawn, as I have already demonstrated, that it was otherwise.

Now I shall deal with Vibhishana. The Aryans have translated him to the position of an Alwar or a saint, and counted him amongst the limited members of Siranjeevies or immortals. He is even supposed to rule over Ceylon, of which fact the British Government is not cognizant, and I am not aware that they are paying any tribute to him. It does not appear what virtue Mr. Sadasiva Iyer has detected in him when he states that he fought strenuously on the side of Rama. But a Dravidian certainly finds in him a most ambitious, ungrateful, unbrotherly and disloyal individual. No doubt he counselled against war on the ground of overwhelming strength on the Aryan side. There were, however, others who did the same and yet stood firm by their king, father, brother and lord, and their country. For instance, Kumbhakarna, the mightiest of Ravana's brothers, while agreeing with Vibhishana in denouncing the conduct of Ravana in abducting Sita (as given by the Aryan chronicler), was determined to be "True to brother, and to monarch, be he right, be he wrong" and “to fight for Lanka.” Mr. Dutt speaking of these brothers in his Ramayana makes the following observations:—

“It is noticeable that Ravan’s second brother, Kumbhakarna, had the courage to censure his elder’s action. But unlike Bibhishan he was determined to fight for his king whether he was right or wrong. There is a touch of sublimity in the devoted loyalty of Kumbhakarna” (Vide noted prefix to Book IX of Dutt’s Ramayana page 127). Though the Ramayana does not state so, it appears to me that Vibhishana was already in communication with the hostile camp to play his act of treachery for the sake of the coveted crown of Ravana. For, this fact is apparent from the abrupt manner in which Vibhishana deserted Ravana with four of his ministers and went over to the enemy, though considerable efforts have been made by the chronicler to show that he was first suspected as a spy, and that it was only after considerable deliberation he was admitted into the confidence of Rama and his party (Vide cantos 17 and 18, Yudhakanda). After he joined Rama, the greatest service Vibhishana rendered was by informing him from time to time of “the secrets by which each warrior could be killed.” To enable him to play his part successfully, with the aid of his intimate knowledge of his kinsmen, he watched the movements of every one of them, obtained all useful information, and communicated it to the enemies of his country whenever they stood in need of it. The death of Indrajit for instance—the most tragic of all the incidents in this war—was brought about in this fashion; For, he was known to be invincible, and he would not have been entrapped had he not been taken by surprise at an unguarded moment, by Lakshmana, acting on the information furnished by Vibhishana (Vide cantos 85 to 91, Yudhakanda see also canto 35 of the Uttarakanda). Thus the greatest of traitors, whom every Dravidian that has in him a spark of patriotism ought to execrate, has been raised to the status and dignity of an Alwar. In our days we have heard of men selling plans of fortifications and ships of naval warfare to the enemies of their country, and how they have been dealt with when found out. In the Rama-Ravana war, if the tables had only been turned against the Aryans, the fate of Vibhishana could be easily imagined. At its conclusion, there was the usual mock lamentation on the part of this Judas at the fall of Ravana but the fact that he assumed purple without loss of time and without trying to place a direct descendant of Ravana on the throne exhibits him in his true light.

Ravana.—In regard to the character of Ravana I have not much to add to what I have stated in my first article. Mr. Sadasiva Iyer has made out a long list of his disqualifications as a man and a king and of heinous crimes committed by him. But the readers of the Ramayana are familiar with the austere penance he performed for a great length of time accompanied with such self-sacrifice as was unknown to Aryans (Canto 32, Aranyakanda and canto 10, Uttarakanda.) This was at the beginning of his career, but his subsequent life shows that he allowed not a single day to pass without worshipping the Siva-linga with the aid of the choicest flowers and sandal (Canto 36, Uttarakanda). His piety is also exemplified by the innumerable hymns he sang, set to music, in honour of Siva at Kailas (Canto 16, Uttarakanda.) He was also versed in the foreign lore of the Vedas, Angas, and Sastras (Canto 32, Aranyakanda). In addition to music he was also a patron of the other fine arts, as will be seen from the fact that they had attained perfection in his dominions. Certainly the character of the individual who fosters these cannot be depraved. The Ramayana does not speak of any internal troubles in the kingdom though there were expeditions of conquest beyond its confines and all round the known world. But he lived in peace with his brother Dravidian kings such as Vali of Kishkindha and Arjuna of Mâhishmati on the banks of the Narbada (Cantos 37 and 39, Uttarakanda,) and his quarrel appears to have been only with the foreigners. I shall not further tire the reader by enumerating his virtues. In short, the fear of God and other concomitant virtues improve the best side of human nature and are inconsistent with the picture drawn of him by his enemies. Once upon a time, a tiger and a man met together to witness a painting in which a ferocious tiger was represented as being trampled under the foot of a man. The individual referred to above naturally addressing the beast taunted it pointing out how a fellow tiger was being treated by his brother man. The curt reply the tiger gave was that the picture was drawn by a man. It is necessary to regard the account of Valmiki in the strain of this anecdote. Ravana, therefore, in the light of the statements of the Aryans themselves, was one of the highest and the noblest specimens of humanity and he was misrepresented with an object. My friend Mr. V. P. Subramania Mudaliar observes most ingeniously but truly, that the unnatural possession of the ten heads and twenty arms by Ravana did not literally mean so but only went to show that he had the best qualities of the head and heart, and that foreign jealousy would not permit them to be shown in their true light. It is no wonder therefore, that Sita, who fell into the clutches of Ravana as a prisoner of war, was safe in his hands, notwithstanding the fact that he was over head and ears in love with her. It was quite in his power to violate her chastity, but he would not do anything of the kind against her will and pleasure. It was for this reason he laboured directly and through others to win her affection. Canto 31 of the Uttarakanda threatens a curse against him if ever he dares to violate the modesty of a woman. It seems that this malediction arose out of his unauthorised conduct towards Rambha—the chief of the prostitutes of the dominions of Indra. In the first place, the story is improbable, as she would only have been too glad to secure the love of one who was all-powerful in all the three worlds. In the next place, it was a subterfuge invented by the Aryans to belittle the magnanimity of a great and good man. Lastly, supernaturalism does not find a place in a historical criticism.

There are one or two other points raised by Mr. Sadasiva Iyer respecting the character of Ravana which should not go unchallenged. He says that he was an undutiful son and an unnatural brother referring to his dealings with Kubera. Both were sons of Visrava, the son of Pulasthya, but by different mothers, one the daughter of Baradwaja and the other of Sumali the Rakshasa. From the birth of time Lanka was the heritage of the Rakshasas, but ewing to the insolence offered by them to the celestials, they were driven out of it to the nether world. When Kubera was about to be settled in life, he wanted a place to reside, and, Pulasthya, his grandfather, asked him to occupy the deserted city of Lanka, (Canto 3, Uttarakanda). While he was in possession of it, Ravana attained to man's estate and his maternal grandfather Sumali instigated him to claim it. On this, Kubera consulted their common father Visrava, and he advised him to give it up and retire to the side of Kailas. I do not see any impropriety in claiming one's ancestral estate from an usurper; there is nothing unfilial or unbrotherly in doing so. With regard to the Pushpakavimana belonging to Kubera, he was deprived of it by Ravana in a fair fight. One day the former sent an insulting message to the latter respecting his conduct towards the celestials. He took umbrage at this, fought with him and carried away his Pushpakavimana as a trophy of victory (Canto 15, Uttarakanda).

The abduction of Sita.—Though, in order to meet the arguments of my critic, I have here and there taken for granted the mythological accounts given by Valmiki, to examine this question impartially it is necssary that my readers should shake off the halo of divinity that surrounds certain characters and the allegorical veil thrown over certain portions of the Ramayana. It will then be conceded, in the first place, that Tadaka was connected with the royal family of Lanka at least as a member of the Rakshasa race, if she was not even more closely allied, and her death therefore by the hand of Rama must have been working in the minds of all prominent Rakshasas, as she was herself a leading member of the community, having been the powerful queen of a province of India. In the next place, Surpanaka was a princess holding a high status at Dandakaranya and Janasthana. She was married to the king of Danavas, but in a war that ensued between those people and Ravana, he was killed by Ravana himself (Canto 23, Uttarakanda). On the complaint of his widowed sister, she was appointed as the Vicerene of the two provinces named above. Kara was nominated as her Prime Minister to carry out her behests and Dushana was deputed at the head of 14,000 men to guard her and her kingdom (Vide Canto 29, Uttarakanda.) When there exist chapter and verse for the statement made by me in the very authority on which Mr. Sadasiva Iyer relied, I cannot conceive how he could convict us of misquotations and claim that the provinces formed a part of the kingdom of the Ikshvakus. But this is a digression. To resume the thread of the account, Ravana must have felt the mutilation of the features of his unfortunate sister as an insult added to injury. To add to these, the kingdom was laid waste and the garrison of 14,000 picked men was annihilated. Further the enemies of his (Ravana's) country, who were under a ban not to enter it, were encouraged to cross the borders and settle themselves down with impunity. These series of events are sufficient as a casus beli, and Ravana was therefore justified in retaliating upon Rama by carrying away Sita. As I have already stated, conditions of war both in ancient and modern times permitted such a course. To say that the all-powerful Ravana went like a thief, when there was no necessity for such a course, and that Surpanaka rushed upon Sita at an unguarded moment in order to eat her up are unlikely and incredible stories. When Ravana knew that the flower of his army was destroyed, he would have gone to the scene of the battle with a large re-inforcement and not single-handed. In all probability Rama and Lakshmana were discomfited before Sita was captured, and, in order to screen a great disgrace, fanciful stories were concocted. In the same way the royal princess who was ruling over Dandakaranya and Janasthana could not have gone to snatch away Sita unattended. It is likely that she was in love with Rama and, impelled by this, she paid a clandestine visit to him, and being detected by Sita, Lakshmana treated her in the manner described above at her instance. It may be that Rama passed over the matter as a freak on the part of an idiotic craven crone, but the manner in which this refined torture was perpetrated on the person of a woman, shows that the idea could only have emanated from another woman impelled by feelings of fiendish revenge. But whoever may have been their author, such acts of barbarity did not become any polished man, much less Rama, who had put on the garb of the universal avenger of wrongs.

In my first paper, I had raised a number of questions which call for historical criticism, but Mr. Sadasiva Iyer has thought fit to dismiss them with the simple statement that he was not going to criticise the logic and conclusions arrived at by me as I have already stated. I have referred to the existence of Rakshasas, Asuras, Devas and Vanaras. It requires no long arguments to prove that, in God's kingdom, there was no catylysm of this kind. Everything has always been in its normal condition, and if there was anything unnatural, it was the mind of man that brought about that aberration incited by malice and envy. We will take for instance the Rakshasas and see if such beings as described by Valmiki were ever created. If my readers would take the trouble of referring to canto 4 of the Uttarakanda of the Ramayana, they would find that in the beginning God created water, and then men to guard it. When he assigned this duty they said rakshânâm, "we will protect." Thus even according to the mythological accounts of the Aryans. Rakshasa was a man and he was created to be the guardian of property. In Southern India there is a class of stalwart dark complexioned people called Marravas, meaning heroes, breathing martial spirit in them and always in search of adventures, and of whom every Dravidian has reasons to feel proud (notwithstanding the bad habits into which some of them have fallen of late). I think it was to them that the early Aryans have referred as Rakshasas. They were either aboriginal inhabitants of the place or the earliest settlers. They not only formed the fighting strength of the early sovereigns, but were also engaged in policing the country in peaceful times, besides being rulers of provinces. From a 'certain noble duty they had to perform, and that during nights, the Aryans chose to nickname them and add a reproach to it. All this, as well as the assigning of superhuman strength to them, was meant to enhance the reputation of the Aryans. For, if it can be said that an ordinary mortal killed in a fair fight a giant of the status of Virathan, who moved about like a fleeting mountain, carrying in his train all kinds of monsters and being decked with garlands of elephants, lions and other animals of the wood without number, strung together by means of serpents of immense size (Canto 4, Aranyakanda) the credit is all his. In the same way, if it is represented that Rama, a child in his teens, fought Tadaka of the description given in canto 25 of the Balakanda, and that he killed Ravana of twenty arms, his reputation must spread throughout the world vide also Sabhaparva—Mahabaratha. In the same way, the origin of Asuras and Vanaras who belonged to a prior wave of emigration may be traced as I have already stated, the Devas and Rishis were only sections of the Aryans who were introduced into the Dravida land. Mr. Sadasiva Iyer omitted to refer to this subject or ignored it, so that an unpleasant truth might not be laid bare before that portion of the public who are held in a spell of ignorance.

In conclusion, I regret that this paper has run out to this inordinate length against my expectations. In performing a duty to the public, for I regard it as such, if I have exceeded the limits of an ordinary magazine article, I have only to crave the indulgence of my readers, and, in atonement of my sin, I make the following summary.

1. That my paper on the Ramayana was a historical criticism and it did not deal with any faith or attack of any class.

2. That the intemperate language in which Mr. Sadasiva Iyer's review is couched and the introduction of politics into the discussion were uncalled for—particularly in the present unfortunate condition of India.

3. That the Dravidians belonged to a wave of emigration earlier than that of Aryans and they had a civilization distinctly their own.

4. That there is certainly Aryan blood in the Dravidians while Dravidian blood runs free in the veins of Aryans.

5. That the caste system in Southern India was of later introduction than in the north.

6. That the want of faith in the Ramayana on the part of the late professor Sundaram Pillai continued to the day of his death.

7. That the Ikshvakus never exercised imperial authority over the whole India, much less over Dandakaranya and Janasthana which were under the absolute control of Ravana. There is internal evidence in the Ramayana besides extraneous circumstances to prove this fact.

8. That Tadaka was of the same race as Ravana even if she did not stand in the relationship of a grandmother to him.

9. That in espousing the cause of Sugriva, Rama did not espouse a right cause. Vali was a more virtuous person than his brother.

10. That both the reasons advanced by Rama for killing Vali from his place of concealment are untenable.

11. That Vibhishana was the greatest traitor to his country, besides being disloyal and unbrotherly.

12. That, Ravana and his tribe of Rakshasas belonged to the human race and, in all probability, to the Marava community of the present day, thus forming a section of the Dravidians; and (Ravana) was the highest and the noblest specimen of humanity of his time.

13. That the so-called abduction of Sita, was only her capture as a prisoner of war and the act of Ravana is justified both by ancient and modern laws of warfare.

KUTTALAM,
28th January, 1910. }

T. PONNAMBALAM PILLAI.

The Morality of the Ramayana—A Rejoinder.

BY

MR. T. PONNAMBALAM PILLAI, M. R. A. S.

In preparing my paper on the Morality of Ramayana, to the “Malabar Quarterly Review” I intended to interpret the views of the late professor Sundaram Pillai, to a larger circle of readers than the Tamil article, in the Tamilian Antiquary, (No. 2), was able to command, in order to elicit rational criticism, in the interests of the Southern Indian History. As education advances it is but natural that investigations into the history of one’s own land, particularly if it is enveloped in mystery, should be made. At all events, such a spirit pervades at present the minds of all educated men both in Southern India and Ceylon, where most of the scenes in the Ramayana have been laid. If in the course of such a legitimate enquiry old ideas are exploded, all right thinking people ought to welcome such a healthy change, and sympathise with the workers in their difficult labours. In the place of such generous treatment, I least expected a furious, but a pointless attack, from the pen of Mr. Sadasiva Iyer, the talented Chief Justice of Travancore, who is known for his perfect equanimity of temper, and who until now never permitted it to be ruffled by anything, as became an arbiter of Justice in the Highest Court of the kingdom. I also regret, that in the heat of the fight he should have so forgotten himself, as to introduce into the arena of discussion, a large number of unparliamentary expressions (about 40 in number besides unlimited inuendoes), thus following the vernacular controversies he has condemned after taking exception to my using certain strong terms; and as a crowning act, that he should have suggested, that some evil spirit, probably from the nether world, impelled me to set my pen to the article in question.
